Where it began

Paul Collingwood was born on 26 May 1976 in Shotley Bridge, near Consett in County Durham, and grew up there. He first played at school, and was good enough to get into the Shotley Bridge under-13 side when he was nine.

He joined Durham, his home county, in 1995, at first seen as a bowler who could bat a little. On his first-class debut in 1996, against Northamptonshire at the Riverside, he took a wicket with his first ball and made 91. A season in Melbourne club cricket with Richmond in 2000–01 sharpened him further, and he came home sharing the Jack Ryder Medal, the league's award for its finest player.

The player

He first played for England in one-day cricket in 2001 and won his first Test cap at Galle in December 2003. For a while he was mostly the man carrying the drinks on tours, until he was called up for the decisive last match of the 2005 Ashes. From 2006 he was a fixture.

In 68 Tests up to 2011 he made 4,260 runs at 40.57 with ten hundreds, and took 96 catches. The innings most people remember is his 206 at Adelaide in the 2006–07 series, the first double hundred by an Englishman in Australia since Wally Hammond, made during a stand of 310 with Kevin Pietersen. He finished his Test career on a happy note, as part of the side that won in Australia in 2010–11, his third Ashes win.

What made him special

Grit and his hands. Nasser Hussain called him Brigadier Block for his defence, and in Cardiff in 2009 he batted for nearly the whole last day, 74 from 245 balls, to help save a Test that looked lost. In the field he was one of the best of his time, at backward point or in the slips, and he could even keep wicket when asked.

In one-day cricket he was England's most capped player for a decade, and in 2005 he made 112 not out and took 6 for 31 against Bangladesh, the first man to do both in one ODI. His Test bowling was the quieter side of his game: 17 wickets, and one spell of off-spin that puzzled even the Test Match Special commentators.

Away from the middle

In 2010 he captained England to the World Twenty20 title, their first global trophy, and hit the winning runs in the final. Wisden made him a Cricketer of the Year in 2007, and he was appointed MBE. He captained Durham to the County Championship in 2013, then moved into coaching, with Scotland and then with England as fielding coach, and in 2022 he took charge of the men's Test side as interim head coach. Away from cricket he is a keen Sunderland supporter.

And finally

His team-mates also called him Shep, after the Blue Peter dog. It is hard to think of a better nickname for a man who chased every ball to the boundary.
